transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-01
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 50 minutes
Attendees: Riley Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood Product), Maya Thompson (Praxis CTO), Ethan Cruz (ML Eng), Priya Nair (Security), Carlos Vega (PM)

Auto Summary: Quick product walkthrough of JSON-mode/typed responses, console validation and sandboxed tool invocations. Discussed tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC pilot logistics, security requirements (SOC2, KMS, audit logs). Agreed to pilot with sample prompts and runbook.

[00:00:00] Riley: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Riley from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:00:12] Maya: Maya here.
[00:00:14] Ethan: Ethan, hi.
[00:00:16] Priya: Priya.
[00:00:18] Carlos: Carlos.
[00:00:20] Samir: Samir from SE. Jordan's on as well. Cool.
[00:00:30] Riley: Goal today is a hands-on walkthrough of our JSON-mode / typed-response playbook and how we safely invoke customer tools. We'll show Console sandbox, API examples, and what Optimize recommends for batching/quantization for your workload.
[00:00:37] Maya: Sounds great, main ask is we need predictable outputs for downstream systems and strong guarantees around any tool calls — we can't have the model leaking PII to third-party services.
[00:00:50] Priya: Also need clear audit trails and KMS integration, and confirmation Redwood can run inside our VPC for the pilot.
[00:01:05] Samir: Totally — we'll demo the typed response contracts which make the model output conform to a schema, and runtime guardrails that prevent outbound invokes unless they pass policy checks. Note: sometimes the auto-transcript will say KV cash instead of KV cache, apologies in advance for any mis-words.
[00:01:25] Ethan: Quick question on latency — we're sensitive, p95 under 500ms is ideal for short prompts. Does Redwood support that on Dedicated?
[00:01:35] Riley: Yes. For short prompts we've seen p95 in the 120-300ms range depending on model and quantization. For Dedicated reserved pools you can aim for tighter SLOs; we'll share benchmark runs. Optimize will also recommend batching levels; there's a tradeoff.
[00:02:05] Jordan: I'll pull up the Console — demo mode, note we have a schema editor, runtime mapping, and a sandbox tab that simulates tool invocation without actually hitting external endpoints.
[00:02:22] [Screen share noise] Jordan: Here is a JSON Schema we created for an invoice extraction flow — required fields, types, enumerations. We can attach this schema to a route so all responses are validated at the edge.
[00:02:45] Maya: If the model can't produce valid JSON, does Redwood auto-correct or fallback?
[00:02:51] Samir: Great question. We have a few layered behaviors: first, the model is guided with strict system prompts and examples; second, the Console enforces schema parsing and will attempt safe repairs up to a threshold, then fall back to a typed-safe failure payload. Third, the runtime supports automatic fallback to a deterministic extractor (heuristic/rule) if the schema fails repeatedly. You can configure retries and canary percentages.
[00:03:25] Ethan: That fallback mechanism — is it local or does it call an external microservice? We want to avoid any unapproved external calls.
[00:03:31] Samir: The fallback can be configured to run inside the same private runtime — in VPC/private deployments it's entirely customer-controlled. In hosted mode fallbacks run in Redwood's runtime but we can route to your private function via secure egress if configured.
[00:03:50] Priya: I want to understand the policy checks before tool invoke — how do you prevent a hallucinated URL being called?
[00:03:57] Samir: We run a policy engine: all tool calls are validated against a schema for the tool (inputs/intent), allowlists/blocklists for domains, and an outbound permission hook. The Console sandbox demonstrates the policy failing and shows explicit audit entries. If anything is suspicious it will never leave the runtime — it's blocked and logged.
[00:04:27] Riley: Let's flip to the API example — here's a payload to the /generate endpoint with "json_mode": true, schema attached, and a tool manifest declaring allowed tool verbs. Note the headers for client-key and optional metadata to pin the model version.
[00:04:46] [00:05:05] Samir: While Jordan is loading the API call, quick note: Optimize can recommend quantization (8-bit vs 4-bit), kernel choices and batch sizes. For an invoice-extract workload we recommended A100 with 4-bit quantization for cost/tp balance; but for ultra low latency you'd pick a higher-clock GPU.
[00:05:30] Ethan: Do you have a sample cost estimate for that config?
[00:05:33] Riley: We'll send a pricing sheet in the SOW; ballpark for a mid-sized throughput with dedicated capacity is in the S$/hr range — exact numbers depend on reserved vs burst capacity.
[00:05:50] Maya: Important: data residency — some of our invoices must stay in-region and be encrypted with our keys.
[00:05:58] Samir: For Private/VPC we support customer KMS/HSM references and all data-in-flight uses TLS. Audit logs are delivered to your logging endpoint or S3 bucket and you can enforce retention.
[00:06:18] Priya: SOC2 and ISO certs?
[00:06:22] Riley: Yes, SOC2 Type II available. We'll attach the security whitepaper and the SOC2 report to the follow-up.
[00:06:35] [00:07:10] Jordan: Back to the Console sandbox: here's a simulated tool invocation where the model returns a payload that attempts to call external URL "http://malicious.example". The sandbox policy blocks it, marks it as policy_violation, and returns a structured error. You can see the audit trail: timestamp, caller identity, route, matched policy rule.
[00:07:40] Carlos: Nice — can we integrate that audit trail into our SIEM?
[00:07:43] Samir: Yes, we have webhooks and syslog/S3 exports, you can route events to your SIEM, and we support structured event schemas.
[00:08:05] Maya: For pilot success criteria — we want 99% structured success on our core invoice prompt set, p95 < 500ms, and no outbound invokes to unapproved domains. Is that realistic?
[00:08:18] Riley: Realistic as a pilot. 99% structured success is achievable with prompt engineering + schema enforcement + fallback rules. We'll instrument evaluation and regressions with Redwood Optimize and tie alerts to a prompt set.
[00:08:40] Ethan: About rollout — we prefer a canary to 10% traffic first. Can Redwood do canary + auto-fallback to previous model?
[00:08:48] Samir: Yes, Console supports canary % rollouts, A/B testing, automatic metric-based rollback. You can also pin routes to model versions.
[00:09:10] [00:09:55] Riley: Let's show an API sample for typed invoke: payload includes "tools": [{"name":"fetch_invoice","schema":...}] and "invoke_mode":"sandbox" or "live". In sandbox no external calls occur and you get an execution plan back. In live mode the runtime validates and then executes.
[00:10:18] Priya: Does sandbox simulate network latency or just logic?
[00:10:22] Jordan: Primarily logic — it simulates responses and policy outcomes. We can also run replay tests that hit a staged endpoint to validate latency.
[00:10:40] Ethan: About observability: can we get token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route?
[00:10:46] Riley: Yes, Console has token-level charts, per-route p50/p95, and cost attribution per model. You can export these as CSV/JSON.
[00:11:10] [00:11:35] Maya: On the private deploy side, ops wise what do you need from us?
[00:11:40] Samir: We'll need VPC peering details or a VPN, a service account with minimal privileges for deployment orchestration, access to your KMS wrapping key info, and a CIDR range for the runtime. We provide an install manifest and a runbook.
[00:12:05] Carlos: How long is a typical pilot to prove performance?
[00:12:09] Riley: Usually 3-6 weeks: week 1 integration and sample prompts, week 2 benchmarks and tuning, week 3-4 feature validation and canary ramp. We can compress if you have resources.
[00:12:30] [00:12:45] Priya: Any legal or procurement blockers we've seen?
[00:12:48] Riley: Standard entitlements, DPAs, and security questionnaires. For on-prem/private we add an additional software license addendum. We'll work with your procurement on the SOW.
[00:13:05] Ethan: A technical nit — when the model returns JSON that includes a tool call, how do you ensure the arguments are safe? E.g., no personally identifying info gets passed to a third-party enrichment API.
[00:13:18] Samir: We support input redaction policies and argument schemas: you can drop fields, mask them, or require explicit allow-headers. Also runtime will not forward if the argument set contains sensitive flags unless the route explicitly allows it.
[00:13:40] Maya: Will you ship a sample policy we can iterate on?
[00:13:44] Samir: Yes, we'll include a starter policy pack for finance workflows.
[00:13:55] [00:14:30] Jordan: Demoing the failure path now — model produces malformed JSON; Console shows parse errors and a suggested repair. If you elect "enforced", the runtime returns a typed error and does not invoke any tool. If you elect "repair", it will attempt deterministic correction up to three times.
[00:14:55] Carlos: How noisy are the repair attempts in logs? We don't want a flood.
[00:14:59] Samir: Repairs are aggregated in the audit logs with counts and sample payloads, and you can toggle verbosity.
[00:15:20] [00:15:40] Riley: Quick check — what are Praxis's capacity needs?
[00:15:45] Ethan: Expected 10k invoice extracts/day initially, peaks to ~50k/day during month close; concurrency spikes matter.
[00:15:55] Riley: For that footprint we usually recommend a small dedicated pool with autoscale burst; Optimize will provide exact GPU-hour estimates for throughput targets.
[00:16:12] Maya: One more security detail — do you support SAML SSO and SCIM for RBAC?
[00:16:17] Samir: Yes SAML SSO for Console access, SCIM provisioning for users and RBAC.
[00:16:30] [00:17:05] Priya: For the VPC pilot, can logs be pushed to our private S3 and then deleted after a retention period?
[00:17:12] Samir: Yes, logs can be exported to your S3 with configurable retention; we can also keep a short-term copy on Redwood side if requested for debugging, but that is an explicit setting.
[00:17:35] Riley: Let's run a quick live sandbox for a sample prompt: Ethan will paste the invoice prompt.
[00:17:40] Ethan: Pasting...
[00:17:52] [typing, 00:18:05] Jordan: Sandbox run: model responded with structured JSON, tool invocation flagged for external enrichment domain. Policy blocked and returned structured error. See sample payload in the console.
[00:18:30] Ethan: Ok seeing it. The error payload looks good — it's cleanly typed so our downstream parser won't crash.
[00:18:40] Maya: Can we test a live invoke to our enrichment service in a staging env?
[00:18:44] Samir: Yes, via a secure tunnel or peered endpoint; we'll do replay tests to measure true p95.
[00:18:58] [00:19:20] Jordan: Quick note on model pinning: you can pin a route to a specific model version and only allow upgrades via a rollout in the Console. This avoids silent quality shifts.
[00:19:40] Riley: All right, nearing the end — let's recap next steps and owners.
[00:19:48] Riley: Action items: we'll send SOW/pricing, security docs, and the VPC runbook. Samir will draft pilot config and starter policy. Maya/Ethan will share prompt set and perf targets. Priya will send compliance Qs.
[00:20:05] Maya: Timeline: aim to start integration week of 11/8.
[00:20:10] Riley: Works for us. Anything else?
[00:20:14] Carlos: Can we get a brief benchmark CSV from a similar customer?
[00:20:18] Samir: I'll include a sanitized benchmark example in the follow-up.
[00:20:25] Priya: Please include the exact audit event schema.
[00:20:28] Samir: Will do.
[00:20:35] Riley: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the packet.
[00:20:40] Maya: Thanks.
[00:20:43] [call ends]

Post-meeting notes: Customer is security conscious and wants VPC pilot. They prioritize structured success and auditability over raw throughput initially. Pilot scope looks like 3-week integration and tune, followed by gradual canary.
